sections.heading: Shiva Bhoramdeo Temple
sections.content: Early Medieval 7-11th Centaury The Maikal mountains are home to the Bhoramdeo temple, which is carved on the rocky stones in the Nagara style. This temple was built around seventh to eleventh century CE. The Bhoramdeo temple has a resemblance with the Sun temple of Konark and the Khajuraho temple. The temple is unique for its architecture. Sir Alexander Cunningham was a British archaeologist and army engineer, had termed it as one of the most beautifully decorated temples seen by him.The main temple here has two parts. One is known as Ishtika made temple and the other is completely stone-carved. This medieval temple has been constructed upon a five feet high sprawling platform including a mandapa, antarala and garbhagriha. The mandapa has a square shape having four pillars in the centre and the rest are in periphery, associated with high roofs. There is a half shelter also on each entrance. In the garbhagriha a Shiva Linga is situated. The outer walls are adorned with the sculptures of Lord Vishnu and his other incarnations, besides those of Shiva, Ganesha etc. The row of idols from top to bottom have a size of one, one and half, and two feet height respectively. The bottom part of the temple has four structures to keep the main body of the temple .The idols of elephants and lions queued up on the top give the temple a decorative look. The main idols in the temple are those of Uma-Maheswar, Nataraj, Narsimha, Vaman, Krishna, Surya, Kaal, Bhairava, Nritya Ganesh, Kartikeya, Tandul, Shivgang, Chamunda, Ambika, Saptamatrika and Laxmi-Naryan. The traces of Ramkatha are also engraved here in stones. Amidst a variety of idols the carnal sculptures of the temple are appreciated for their exquisite carving in different erotic poses, obviously to reflect the lifestyle of those historic periods.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Monument- Dantewada
sections.content: A very ancient town of India, Dantewada derives its name from the capital town of the district, named after the presiding deity of the town Ma Danteshwari. Earlier this town was known as Tarlapal and Dantawali, mention of which can be found on the stone carvings found in the district. A splendid temple of Goddess Danteswari is the highlight of this town. It is one of the Shaktipithas which is visited by devotees from different parts of the country through out the year. Constructed, mainly in the south Indian style (Dravida) architecture, and located at the confluence of the holy rivers Shankini and Dhankini, this temple gives a pleasant feeling of peace and immense satisfaction to the minds of devotees.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Handicrafts - Bamboo Craft
sections.content: Chhattisgarh has a very wide variety of bamboo grown in the state and the craftspersons of the state make excellent bamboo items. Articles for daily as well as decorative use are produced by the local tribal artisans. Some of the well known bamboo products of the state include agricultural implements, fishing traps, hunting tools and baskets.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Handicrafts - Woodwork
sections.content: The craftspeople of Chattisgarh make beautiful decorative wood carvings. The skillful craftsmen of the state carve beautiful wooden ceilings, doors, lintels etc using different kinds of wood like shisham, teak, dhudi, sal and kikar. The craftsmen also make pipes, masks, doors, window frames and sculptures.

sections.heading: Jewellery
sections.content: from Chhattisgarh is crafted in a variety of silver, bronze and mixed metal. Ornament made out of beads, cowries and feathers are part of tribal costumes. Tribal men and women wear traditional ornaments that are very attractive and colourful.

sections.heading: Metalcraft
sections.content: Bastar is inhabited by the most exotic tribes of India. It is richly endowed with minerals and forest resources. Bastar is, predominantly, a forest area, and home of Marias and Murias, both extremely colorful and picturesque tribes, who have preserved their ancient culture. The lohars of Kondagaon village in Bastar have been engaged in iron craft for generations and indulge in making of farm implements, lamps and other household objects. The iron objects are made by hammering them into shape; they are not cast or moulded. The hot iron is beaten repeatedly to the desired shape while the unnecessary portion is cut away and filed to remove the sharp edges. Hollow images usually bigger than solid ones are made out of beaten iron sheets, folded, cut, and filed to shape the deepak (lamps), and vertical and horizontal rods or strips. These are ornamented with bird and animal figures that are made separately and later joined together into various types of composite lamps. Depending on the variations in structure and use, there are five types of lamps: laman diya, supali diya, gadli diya, khut diya and viman diya.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Handicrafts - Dhokra work
sections.content: Bastar and Raigarh districts of Chhatisgarh create Dhokra crafts from bell metal, brass and bronze. Dhokra essentially refers to the casting of bell metal or bass using the lost-wax technique. In Chhattisgarh, it is the Ghadwa community that is associated with this craft. In local etymology, Ghadwa means to shape or create. A variety of products are crated by the Ghadwas for local use such as images of local gods and deities, vessels, and jewellery. The method of lost wax procedure or cire perdue is used to cast bronze articles. carpenters. Mutni, sooja, pinachaku, hatwani, chimta are few of the tools. Though Dhokra casting is used across the globe, the coiled thread technique is unique to Bastar. The traditional lost wax technique is simple and ideal for use in tribal settings. The craftsman begins by winding a slim thread of wax over the contours of a clay core. It is then thickly coated with fine clay obtained from termite bills, and baked on drying, leaving a narrow vent to melt away the wax. The vacuum created between the core and the clay layer is filled with molten metal, which is then allowed to cool down and solidify. Then the outer clay mould is cracked open, revealing the beauty of the final sculpture. Simple as this whole process seems, it requires great precision and skill. The metal must be able to flow uniformly and freely through the narrow spaces, and replace the wax without forming any bubbles or gaps. Cow dung, paddy husk and red soil are also used in the manufacture of Dhokra artifacts. Of all the raw materials used by the Ghadwas, the most important is beeswax. Besides the essential contouring, wax wires and pieces are also used for decorations required for finishing the artifacts. It is used because of its extraordinarily high plastic content and pliability. Examples of lost wax casting are practiced all over the world, but the coiled thread technique is unique to Bastar. A glance at the traditional baskets provides a clue to its origin. The basket makers would wind grass around a rope, which was then coiled into shape. The same technique was translated into metal only much later, with forest dwellers being dependent on natural product long before they began to use metal. Metal anklets with basket weave motifs, and beautiful containers reminiscent of wicker baskets also point towards such a transition.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Handicrafts - Silk Weaving
sections.content: Chattisgarh produces excellent quality of silks. Raigarh and Champa are the main silk producing centres.The craftspersons perform traditional and contemporary work. Embroidery is the main attraction on the silk fabrics and there are stitches which are as old as 150 years. Marabhai is one of the traditional embroidery which maintains all its traditional stitches and its a form of hand embroidery. Kosa and Ahimsa are the other most commonly used. The silk thread for the weave is obtained from the jungles of Chhattisgarh without killing the silkworms and involves using crushed and dried Mahuwa seeds to trap the silkworms after the formation of the cocoons.

sections.heading: Madai Festival
sections.content: This festival is popularly celebrated by the Maria Gonds of Bastar to meet relatives settled in different villages across the state. The tribal Goddess is honored by offering the sacrifice of a goat beneath the sacred village tree. The nights are marked with merriment like singing, drinking and dancing. Madai of Narayanpur in Bastar is famous.

sections.heading: Chhattisgarh  Fairs and Festivals - Dussehra
sections.content: The most important festival in the region is a ten days celebration of Dusshera. This festival is believed to have been originated in the fifteenth century by the fourth Kakatiya monarch, Maharaj Purushottam Deo. Almost all the inhabitants of the state participate in this festival. They celebrate Dussehra as a congregation of Maoli Devi and all her sisters. Numerous pujaris (priests) bring local deities beautifully embellished with vibrant colored flowers to the Danteshwari Temple on rathas (chariots) in Jagdalpur. This festival has an underlying spirit of participation, cutting across caste and creed, which prevails. The Dussehra rath, is always pulled by Maria and Dhruva people. The construction of the rath is always exclusively done by the Saoras every year. The iron nails used in the construction of the wooden rath are made by Lohars (blacksmiths).The ropes for dragging the rath are prepared and supplied by the member of the Parja tribe. The construction of the rath is supervised by the Dhakada. Before using the rath for the ceremony it is always worshipped by the members of the Khaki caste.
